routes.description: Establish that biblical truth is properly assessed through genre, revelation, human testimony, and established interpretive tradition, and that textual variation or morally difficult passages need not defeat its historical, theological, moral, or revelatory claims.
routes.successCriteria: Connect an account of revelation and human transmission to affirmative historical or cosmological support, while explaining why apparent contradictions and difficult moral texts do not undermine the Bible's governing truth claims.

motionBridge.description: Show that the Bible remains true in its governing revelatory and theological purpose while retaining sufficient historical and moral credibility across its diverse genres.

centralBridges.description: Define biblical truth through revelation, genre, authorial purpose, and human expression rather than requiring uniform literal or scientific precision.
Establish that cumulative testimony and external corroboration support the historical credibility of the biblical narratives despite nonidentical details.
Explain morally troubling texts through moral development, fulfillment, and the established interpretive practice of living Christian communities.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use claimed convergence between Genesis and later cosmological inquiry as supporting evidence for revelation.
Distinguish ordinary testimonial variation from central falsification and explain why miraculous claims remain possible within the asserted theology.

routes.description: Establish that each biblical claim must meet standards appropriate to its genre and that historical contradictions, theological reshaping, selective evidential methods, and morally troubling divine commands undermine the Bible's asserted forms of truth.
routes.successCriteria: Demonstrate that the principal historical, revelatory, and moral claims face unresolved contradictions or counterexamples that cannot be answered merely by invoking genre, possibility, later tradition, or beneficial reception.

motionBridge.description: Show that contradictions and morally troubling texts materially undermine the Bible's historical, moral, theological, allegorical, or revelatory truth claims.

centralBridges.description: Separate the Bible's genres and require attempted historical reports, moral teachings, and allegories to satisfy the standards appropriate to each claim.
Show that Gospel discrepancies, textual development, and theological reshaping reduce confidence in the narratives used to support central Christian events.
Show that divinely authorized killing and slavery remain incompatible with asserted biblical moral authority despite later reinterpretation or moral development.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require consistent treatment of favorable and unfavorable scientific, archaeological, and textual details when inferring revelation or reliability.
Distinguish the logical possibility of miracles from evidence that specifically biblical miracle reports occurred.

sections.title: Standards of Truth, Genre, and Revelation
sections.rationale: This issue fixes the governing standards for evaluating a diverse scriptural library, including the roles of authorial purpose, human expression, revelation, allegory, and inherited interpretation.

sections.title: Gospel Historicity, Contradictions, and Transmission
sections.rationale: The historical reliability of the Gospels is a principal motion-level clash because discrepancies, editorial development, cumulative testimony, and theological shaping bear directly on central Christian events.

sections.title: Cosmology, Archaeological Corroboration, and Miracles
sections.rationale: Affirmative appeals to scientific anticipation, archaeological detail, and miraculous possibility must be weighed against alternative explanations and limits on what mundane corroboration can establish.

sections.title: Divine Violence and Biblical Moral Authority
sections.rationale: Commands involving conquest and the killing of noncombatants create a direct test of claimed divine moral authority and of whether development, fulfillment, or interpretive tradition resolves difficult texts.

sections.title: Slavery, Moral Development, and Abolitionist Reception
sections.rationale: Biblical slave laws, later teachings, abolitionist use, and communal interpretation test whether the canon presents coherent moral development or contains unresolved moral instability.

chunk-001:c008.proposition: Judging a work's truth requires understanding its genre and purpose, because incidental anachronisms or rearranged events need not defeat the deeper truth the author intends to convey.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-01.proposition: Genesis makes factual claims that the universe began, came from nothing, and was created by God, presenting cosmological assertions that later inquiry can test.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-02.proposition: Revelation is needed because reason cannot answer ultimate questions such as purpose, life after death, and cosmic justice, so faith is not unreasonable when addressing matters beyond reason's limits.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-06.proposition: Ancient Gospel historicity should be judged by the standards of human historical reporting, under which non-eyewitness writers can gather testimony reliably and minor itinerary discrepancies need not defeat a text's purpose.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-10.proposition: The four nonidentical Gospel perspectives should be assessed cumulatively like testimony before a jury, and awkward details such as women discovering the empty tomb give the narratives a ring of authenticity.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-10.proposition: Archaeological discoveries guided by biblical descriptions of David's palace and Sodom and Gomorrah support using the Bible as a source of historical and geographical information.

chunk-004:chunk-004-candidate-06.proposition: The Bible exhibits moral development from Old Testament retaliation to New Testament forgiveness, with fulfillment functioning as transcendence rather than mere repetition of earlier practices.

chunk-004:chunk-004-candidate-08.proposition: Christian moral tradition developed restraints against killing women and children, and contemporary condemnation of such killing draws upon that inherited moral standard.

chunk-004:chunk-004-candidate-10.proposition: Christian abolitionism shows that the Bible's full interpretive tradition can motivate opposition to slavery rather than functioning simply as a defense of it.

chunk-005:c005-02.proposition: A text's significance is substantially shaped by its established communal reading and moral use, and the long abolitionist reception of Exodus weighs against an exclusively oppression-supporting interpretation.

chunk-001:c001.proposition: Because the Bible is a library containing diverse genres, its literal, historical, allegorical, moral, theological, and metaphorical truth claims must be examined separately.

chunk-001:c002.proposition: The Adam and Eve narrative has deficient allegorical coherence because the serpent's prediction appears vindicated while divine banishment and the guarded tree of life require strained explanations.

chunk-001:c003.proposition: Divinely ordered conquest, forced labor, plunder, and the killing of Amalekite children undermine the claim that the Old Testament conveys moral truth.

chunk-001:c006.proposition: Conflicts over the crucifixion date, permitted staff, temple-cleansing chronology, and Mary Magdalene's knowledge are genuine Gospel contradictions that weaken historical reliability.

chunk-001:c007.proposition: Known later interpolations and variant endings demonstrate that Gospel stories were edited, making alteration during oral transmission plausible and weakening their historical reliability.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-08.proposition: Treating Genesis as scientifically prescient about the universe's beginning while dismissing its incorrect ordering of the earth and sun as non-scientific applies inconsistent evidential standards.

chunk-004:chunk-004-candidate-05.proposition: The logical possibility of resurrection or a parted sea provides no evidence that either event occurred and would equally permit rival religious miracle reports.

chunk-004:chunk-004-candidate-07.proposition: New Testament moral development cannot undo divine commands to kill defeated combatants, women, children, and animals in Old Testament conquest narratives.

chunk-004:chunk-004-candidate-09.proposition: Biblical slave law separated enslaved men from wives and children and imposed lifelong slavery despite the availability of a simple, humane moral improvement.

chunk-005:c005-06.proposition: The Old Testament's divine approval of slavery and the New Testament instruction that slaves obey cruel masters leave the Bible morally unstable even if another passage criticized slavery.
